package_info.why_malicious: The driver is a malicious kernel-mode loader that injects shellcode into privileged processes, establishes persistence (including in Safe Boot), monitors and restores its own presence, and ultimately deploys a .NET backdoor with command execution and proxy capabilities. Its behaviors enable remote code execution, persistent access, and covert control of compromised systems.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Find a 32-bit process running as Local System (not in blocklist), open it with ZwOpenProcess(), allocate memory with ZwAllocateVirtualMemory(), and inject embedded shellcode using NtWriteVirtualMemory().
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At driver load, the code locates a suitable privileged process, injects shellcode into its memory, and executes it, enabling execution of arbitrary payloads with SYSTEM privileges.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Kernel drivers should not inject shellcode into user-mode processes, especially with SYSTEM privileges.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate drivers do not perform process injection or arbitrary code execution in other processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security or debugging tools may inject code for monitoring, but never in this covert, privilege-escalating manner.
key_indicators: Use of direct system calls (ZwOpenProcess, NtWriteVirtualMemory)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Create registry keys: \\REGISTRY\\MACHINE\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\WinTapix, \\REGISTRY\\MACHINE\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\SafeBoot\\Minimal\\WinTapix.sys, \\REGISTRY\\MACHINE\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\SafeBoot\\Network\\WinTapix.sys. Monitor these keys with ZwNotifyChangeKey().
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At driver load, the code creates and monitors registry keys to ensure the driver loads at boot and in Safe Boot, and can restore itself if removed.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Persistence in Safe Boot is highly unusual and indicates intent to survive remediation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate drivers rarely, if ever, register themselves for Safe Boot and do not monitor registry keys for self-restoration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate security software may monitor registry keys, but not for self-reinstatement after removal.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Start a thread with PsCreateSystemThread() to monitor the file location of Wintapix.sys using NtNotifyChangeDirectoryFile(). If the driver file is deleted, write it back to the same location.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At driver load, the code spawns a system thread to monitor its own file on disk and restores it if deleted, ensuring persistent presence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-restoration after deletion is a hallmark of malware persistence and anti-forensics.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate drivers do not monitor or restore their own files if deleted.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some advanced security agents may attempt self-repair, but not at the kernel level.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Decrypted Donut shellcode loads and executes an encrypted .NET payload from memory.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After injection, the shellcode decrypts and loads a .NET assembly in memory, enabling execution of the next-stage payload without touching disk.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: In-memory decryption and execution of .NET payloads is a common malware evasion technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code does not inject and execute arbitrary .NET assemblies in this manner.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red-team tools and some advanced security products may use in-memory execution for testing, but not in production environments.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: HTTP listener on IIS server URLs (constructed from decoded arrays). If request contains 'wOxhuoSBgpGcnLQZxipa', respond with 'UsEPTIkCRUwarKZfRnyjcG13DFA'. If request has 'Jet' or ' Ver' parameter, base64-decode and execute as 'cmd /c <command>' and return output. If request body present, decrypt and: (a) execute command, (b) upload file, (c) download file.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the .NET payload acts as a backdoor, listening on specific IIS URLs for commands, executing arbitrary code, and handling file uploads/downloads, all with simple XOR encryption for C2 traffic.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Arbitrary command execution and file transfer over HTTP endpoints is classic backdoor behavior.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate IIS modules do not provide covert command execution or file transfer endpoints.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools may have similar features, but are not covertly injected or hidden.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Proxy listener on IIS URLs (from 'input' array). Accepts data streams, including RDP configuration, and proxies connections to remote RDP servers.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the .NET payload establishes proxy listeners on IIS endpoints, enabling the attacker to tunnel arbitrary data (including RDP sessions) through the compromised host.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Covert proxying of RDP and other data streams is a common lateral movement and C2 technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: IIS servers should not proxy RDP or arbitrary data for external parties.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate reverse proxies exist, but are not covertly injected or hidden in this manner.

attack_chain.action: Malicious driver (WinTapix.sys/SRVNET2.SYS) is loaded into the Windows kernel, possibly via a vulnerable legitimate driver.
attack_chain.leads_to: Kernel-level persistence and setup for code injection.

attack_chain.action: Driver injects embedded shellcode into a privileged 32-bit process running as SYSTEM.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of shellcode in user-mode with high privileges.

attack_chain.action: Injected shellcode decrypts and loads a .NET payload in memory.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of .NET backdoor and proxy functionality.

attack_chain.action: The .NET payload establishes HTTP listeners on IIS endpoints for C2, command execution, file transfer, and proxying (including RDP).
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent, covert remote access and lateral movement capabilities.

attack_chain.action: Driver and registry/file monitoring ensure persistence, self-healing, and resistance to removal.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued presence and re-infection if removal is attempted.

behavioral_signatures: Kernel driver injecting shellcode into user-mode processes
Creation of registry keys for Safe Boot persistence
Monitoring and restoration of driver file and registry keys
In-memory decryption and execution of .NET payloads
IIS HTTP endpoints handling command execution and file transfer
Covert proxying of RDP/data streams via IIS
network_indicators: HTTP requests to non-standard IIS endpoints (constructed from suspicious arrays)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unsigned or suspicious kernel drivers (WinTapix.sys, SRVNET2.SYS) being loaded, especially those creating Safe Boot registry keys. Detect process injection from kernel mode into 32-bit SYSTEM processes. Watch for IIS servers exposing hidden HTTP endpoints that accept commands or proxy RDP. Look for in-memory .NET assemblies loaded by Donut shellcode. Alert on registry/file monitoring and self-restoration behaviors. Correlate with network traffic to unusual IIS paths, especially if carrying XOR-encrypted data or RDP streams.
